title: Slow conversion when loading from CSV and saving as Parquet
body: I am converting 20GB+ CSV datasets to Parquet with DuckDB 0.7.1 on an Apple Silicon M1 iMac with 16GB RAM and a 1TB SSD. Loading a gzip-compressed CSV into an on-disk table takes about three minutes, but copying that table to Parquet takes upwards of three hours. I use read_csv_auto with all_varchar=true and then COPY the table to a Parquet file. Is there a faster way to perform this conversion?

symptoms_visible: Loading the compressed CSV into a DuckDB table takes about three minutes, but writing that table to Parquet takes upwards of three hours.
N0.label: N0 very slow Parquet export reported

symptoms_visible: With the development build and insertion-order preservation disabled, the large all-VARCHAR load completes instead of leaving me with the previous multi-hour workflow.
N1.label: N1 newer build removes initial multi-hour bottleneck

symptoms_visible: A direct conversion of the gzip CSV takes about 550 seconds with either insertion-order setting, and both outputs have the same size.
N2.label: N2 direct conversion benchmarked

symptoms_visible: The fast parallel conversion of the compressed CSV produces only 30,559,373 rows instead of 212,363,079.
The same compressed file returns all 212,363,079 rows with the parallel reader disabled, and the uncompressed CSV returns the full count with parallel reading enabled.
N3.label: N3 compressed parallel reader loses rows

symptoms_visible: After updating to the merged parallel-reader implementation, all of the input appears to load, but reading the resulting Parquet file reports 'No magic bytes found at end of file'.
N4.label: N4 complete input load produces unreadable Parquet

symptoms_visible: The compressed CSV converts to Parquet in about 2 minutes 57 seconds, and the resulting file is readable and contains all 212,363,079 rows.
N_terminal.label: terminal fast and complete conversion verified

solution.intent: Retry the conversion on the latest development build containing the recent VARCHAR-to-Parquet performance improvement, and disable insertion-order preservation to permit parallel Parquet writing.
solution.concrete_example: Build or install the latest DuckDB development version, run SET preserve_insertion_order=false, and repeat the conversion rather than benchmarking the older 0.7.1 writer.
solution.inference_hint: The connection between the all-VARCHAR schema and the recently corrected Parquet-writer performance problem was supplied by the maintainer, not diagnosed by the reporter.

edges.comment: From c4 and reporter c8, all on the reporter's M1 system: a maintainer points to the recent VARCHAR writer improvement and parallel Parquet setting; the reporter installs development build v0.7.2-dev1322 and reports a major improvement.

question_patterns: Can you benchmark a direct COPY from the compressed CSV to Parquet without first creating a persistent table?
How long does the one-pass CSV-to-Parquet conversion take on the newer build?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tried the direct conversion on the development build. It took 549.536 seconds and produced a 4,794,409,184-byte Parquet file.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The direct conversion still takes about three hours on the development build.
The direct conversion takes roughly ten minutes rather than 549.536 seconds.

question_patterns: Please repeat the direct conversion with insertion-order preservation disabled and compare the timing and output size.
Does changing the insertion-order setting speed up this direct conversion?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With insertion-order preservation disabled, it took 551.849 seconds. The two output files are exactly the same size, so this setting did not improve that direct run.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Disabling insertion-order preservation reduces this direct conversion from about nine minutes to under one minute.

question_patterns: What is the expected number of data rows in the source?
Can you count the rows in a known-complete output so later conversions can be checked?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The uncompressed CSV has 212,363,080 lines including the header, and a complete Parquet conversion has 212,363,079 data rows.

edges.comment: Reporter c9 and c11 on the same M1 dataset: direct conversion timings, equal output sizes, and the full expected row count are raw benchmark outputs.

question_patterns: Can you try passing read_csv_auto directly to COPY so you can specify all_varchar, and show the exact result?
What happens when you put the CSV table-function call directly after COPY?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tried COPY read_csv_auto('ccaed182.csv.gz', all_varchar=1) TO ..., but the parser reports a syntax error at the filename.

question_patterns: Can you wrap the CSV reader in a parenthesized SELECT and retry the one-pass conversion?
Does COPY (SELECT * FROM read_csv_auto(...)) let you apply all_varchar successfully?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. COPY (SELECT * FROM read_csv_auto('ccaed182.csv.gz', all_varchar=true)) TO ... works and lets me do the conversion in one command.

question_patterns: Please enable the experimental parallel CSV reader for the compressed input, run the conversion, and count the resulting rows.
What row count do you get when the compressed CSV is read using the parallel setting?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The conversion finished in 31.687 seconds, but the output contains only 30,559,373 rows instead of the full dataset.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The fast output contains all 212,363,079 rows and can be read normally.
The incomplete output contains about 31 million rows rather than exactly 30,559,373.

question_patterns: Repeat the count with the parallel reader disabled; how many rows are returned from the same compressed file?
Does serial reading of the gzip file return the complete dataset?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With the parallel reader disabled, the same gzip file returns all 212,363,079 rows, although the count takes 254.119 seconds.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Serial reading also stops at 30,559,373 rows.

question_patterns: Can you run the same parallel conversion against an uncompressed copy and verify its row count?
Does the incomplete result occur when the CSV is not gzip-compressed?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The uncompressed CSV works with parallel reading: conversion takes 168.212 seconds and the Parquet file contains all 212,363,079 rows.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The uncompressed CSV is truncated to the same row count as the gzip input.

edges.comment: Reporter c12-c23 and c26-c32 on the reporter's dataset: the handler-directed syntax and configuration probes establish raw timings and counts. The conclusion that the old parallel reader mishandles gzip input remains engineer-side.

solution.intent: Update to the newly merged CSV-reader implementation that corrects parallel processing of compressed input, then rerun the complete one-pass conversion and validate the resulting Parquet file.
solution.concrete_example: Build the current source after the parallel CSV reader changes have merged, rerun COPY (SELECT * FROM read_csv_auto(..., all_varchar=true)) TO ... with the large gzip file, and check the output with read_parquet.
solution.inference_hint: Comparing complete serial gzip and parallel uncompressed reads against the truncated parallel gzip read isolates the old compressed parallel-reader implementation; the reporter supplied counts rather than this diagnosis.

edges.comment: Participant4 c33 and reporter c34-c39, all concerning the reporter's dataset: the compressed-reader correction is merged and retested. It fixes the short input load, but the reporter then observes that the produced Parquet files cannot be read because they lack final magic bytes.

solution.intent: Use a build containing the high-memory/OOM correction for the parallel conversion, rerun the one-pass compressed CSV-to-Parquet operation, and verify both Parquet readability and the complete row count before declaring success.
solution.concrete_example: Compile the latest source containing the memory-usage correction, convert the gzip CSV directly to Parquet, then run SELECT count(*) FROM read_parquet(...) and confirm that it returns 212,363,079 rows.
solution.inference_hint: The maintainer determined from the shared workload that high memory usage was invoking the OOM killer and leaving Parquet output without its footer. The reporter's visible evidence was the missing-magic-bytes error; the OOM diagnosis is engineer inference.

edges.comment: Participant2 c40-c41 and reporter c43-c44, all on the original reporter's M1 workload: after the memory correction landed, the reporter compiled a current development build, completed conversion in 177 seconds, and verified that read_parquet returned all 212,363,079 rows.

satisfaction_conditions: Must explain the layered diagnosis: DuckDB 0.7.1 had a severe all-VARCHAR Parquet-writing performance problem, while insertion-order preservation also prevented parallel Parquet writing.
For the requested one-pass conversion, must use a parenthesized SELECT over read_csv_auto so all_varchar can be supplied, rather than requiring a persistent intermediate table.
Must not treat the old experimental parallel reader as a valid fix for gzip input: in the reporter's measurements it returned only 30,559,373 of 212,363,079 rows.
Must identify the final unreadable-Parquet failure as high memory usage leading to the OOM killer and an incomplete file, grounded in the missing-magic-bytes result and maintainer analysis.

Must recommend a build containing both the corrected compressed parallel-reader behavior and the memory-usage correction, then have the reporter verify that the Parquet file is readable and contains all 212,363,079 rows before declaring resolution.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable independent developer who is comfortable compiling DuckDB, running SQL and shell benchmarks, scripting a configuration matrix, and validating file sizes and row counts.
persona_hint.communication_style: Highly enthusiastic, cooperative, and unusually thorough; posts exact commands, timings, counts, file sizes, screenshots, and follow-up benchmark tables.
